National Register of Historic Places listings in Dallas County, Texas
Dealey Plaza (National Historic Landmark District, contributing properties)

stops.name: Dealey Plaza
stops.description: Completed in 1940 as a WPA project where Main, Elm and Commerce funnel together toward the railroad underpass, this park is the ground the world learned by name on November 22, 1963.

stops.name: Texas School Book Depository
stops.description: The Romanesque Revival warehouse facing Dealey Plaza spent years as a county office building and now houses the museum built around the sixth-floor corner window.

stops.name: Dal-Tex Building
stops.description: A seven-story Sullivanesque pile built as an implement warehouse, it stands on the northeast corner of Elm and Houston looking straight across at the Depository.

stops.name: John Fitzgerald Kennedy Memorial
stops.description: Philip Johnson designed this roofless 30-foot square as an open tomb, set one block east of the spot it commemorates and left deliberately empty inside.

stops.name: Dallas County Courthouse
stops.description: Everyone calls the 1891 red sandstone courthouse Old Red; it has traded its courtrooms for a county history museum but kept the turrets.

stops.name: Dallas Union Station
stops.description: Opened in 1916 and now officially Eddie Bernice Johnson Union Station, the terminal still boards Amtrak, DART, commuter rail and streetcar riders a short walk from Dealey Plaza.

stops.name: Reunion Tower
stops.description: Locals just call the 561-foot observation tower The Ball, and its lattice sphere is the one landmark that orients you anywhere in the street grid.

stops.name: Dallas Holocaust and Human Rights Museum
stops.description: The purpose-built galleries opened in 2019 at the southeast corner of Houston and Ross, replacing a cramped storefront the museum had outgrown.

stops.name: Pioneer Plaza
stops.description: Forty-nine bronze longhorns and three mounted trail riders stampede downhill across the block, with Texas ranch brands set into the sidewalk alongside them.

stops.name: Pioneer Park Cemetery
stops.description: Four separate burial grounds established from 1849 grew together into one graveyard here, holding four Dallas mayors and a last interment made in 1921.

stops.name: Dallas City Hall
stops.description: I. M. Pei tipped the whole building outward so every floor overhangs the one beneath it, leaving the front wall leaning over its own plaza.

stops.name: Adolphus Hotel
stops.description: Beer magnate Adolphus Busch opened this Beaux-Arts hotel in 1912 on the site of the old city hall, and for several years it was the tallest building in Texas.

stops.name: Magnolia Hotel
stops.description: The neon Pegasus mounted on this 1922 oil-company headquarters in 1934 outlived the company and became the unofficial emblem of the city.

stops.name: Majestic Theatre
stops.description: Opened for vaudeville in April 1921, it is the last building standing from Theater Row, the stretch of Elm Street that once held the city's movie palaces.

stops.name: Thanks-Giving Square
stops.description: Philip Johnson sank this walled garden fifteen feet below the street to shut out the traffic, and coiled a chapel at one end under a spiral of stained glass.

note: Dallas, TX - first run for this city. Rotation check: the run history shows Atlanta (Jul 29), Baltimore, Boston, Buffalo, Charlotte, Chicago, Cincinnati, Cleveland (Aug 5), then Atlanta AGAIN on Aug 7. That repeat looks like the git --follow failure the job warns about: this checkout is a shallow 50-commit clone with no nightly.json history at all, so the local log is empty and the alphabetically-first city wins by default. I read the history from the GitHub commits API instead of git log. Dallas is the alphabetically first NFL city that has genuinely never run. Worth noting for whoever tunes this job: the shallow clone makes step 1 unreliable by design, and Aug 6 appears to have been missed entirely. All 15 stops sit in a walkable downtown box roughly 1 mile east to west, from Reunion Tower and Dealey Plaza through the West End to the Main Street District, with Pioneer Plaza and City Hall at the south end. Every stop has coordinates on its own Wikipedia article and a street address verified against the NRHP county listing, the article infobox, or an official city source. Every ZIP was looked up rather than assumed. DROPPED: Praetorian Building, which reads as a downtown landmark and was the first skyscraper in Texas, but its infobox status is Demolished and the article is written in the past tense. Two Nominatim ZIP results were wrong and were overridden: '400 Main St, Dallas' matched a Main Street in Garland (75040) rather than Dealey Plaza, corrected to 75202 from the Dallas Park and Recreation facility page; and Dallas City Hall came back 75242, which is a government-only postal code, corrected to 75201 from the city's own contact pages. Pioneer Plaza and Pioneer Park Cemetery deliberately share the address 1428 Young St - that is the official Dallas Parks address for the parcel and the two are contiguous halves of one block, so keep whichever one you want or both. Sources disagree on Dealey Plaza's house number (400 vs 500 Main St); I used 400, which is what the parks department publishes. The Sixth Floor Museum is not filed as its own stop because it occupies the Texas School Book Depository at the same 411 Elm St address. Also skipped, all verified but cut to avoid padding a one-mile loop: Wilson Building, Kirby Building, Main Street Garden Park, Pegasus Plaza, Neiman Marcus Building, Old Dallas Central Library, Dallas Municipal Building. The Confederate War Memorial still appears in the Pioneer Park Cemetery article text as if it were standing; it was removed from the site, so no stop here references it.
